1.why: All five are equally legal groupings of an object collection; nothing in the set is odd in form or scope, so this is a blind pick.

2.why: Only option that both asserts a result and refuses a single cause; the other four are flat single-claim options, and a concede-then-commit shape is the key family in this bank.

3.why: Most specific option (a rate, per batch of forty) among four vaguer payment forms, but the specificity rule is weak on payment sets.

4.why: Of five method changes, halving the survey interval is the one that bears on resolving a first-appearance date, but A is equally available blind.

5.why: A and C are a matched pair (the words did not come from him / he had learned them); the inferential member of such a pair is the key and the concrete member the bait.

6.why: Only qualified-but-committed option (persuaded in outline, not in detail); C and E are absolutes and D is the fence-sit, all three standard distractor families.

7.why: Concede-then-narrow is the one rhetorical act among five that a paragraph is actually built to do; the others are single moves that any paragraph could be said to make.

8.why: The whole option set orbits a firm's misconduct and D names it directly; it also matches the misconduct named in item 22's paired options, a cross-item consistency channel.

9.why: Only option that is both committed and anchored to a specific piece of evidence; B and C are the indifference/fence-sit distractor pair.

10.why: A and B are a reversal pair sharing 'stove' (burned vs kept beside it); I bet the pair contains the key and on the keeping member, but E is an equally specific hiding place.

11.why: Most specific option (flagged, plus a fall, plus a drain) and the only one that carries a functional implication, but a floor-material set is thin ground.

12.why: Vocabulary set; 'reply to' is the common-sense trap and I take the less obvious sense, but nothing in the set decides between 'correspond to' and 'account for'.

13.why: The other four are the modern senses of the headword; 'ample time' is the older sense a prose passage would be testing.

14.why: C and E are a reversal pair about the chamber's use; the key in such a pair is the more inferential and more constrained claim, which is C.

15.why: Four options are interventions and one declines to intervene; the lone member of a different family is the key, and its reason is the only self-justifying one.

16.why: Prefer a two-phase construction claim over a single-phase one, but B is the same shape, so the rule does not resolve to one option.

17.why: C and D are a pair (a witness trusted vs distrusted); I take the plainer member, with low confidence.

18.why: Attitude sets in this bank key to the mild committed option; 'irritation' is the strong-emotion overreach and E is the fence-sit, but D is the only option with external content, which cuts the other way.

19.why: Most specific and most technical grievance in a set about re-cutting a stone, but C is the more human one and equally legal.

20.why: All five are senses of one headword; I take the literary rather than the physical sense, which is a weak default.

21.why: Same headword-sense set; C is the wrong-homonym trap and I take the judgement sense over the physical ones with no basis to choose between the rest.

22.why: C and E are a parallel pair ('includes a group ...'); C names the same misconduct as item 8's strongest option, so the pair resolves to C.

23.why: A is the fence-sit; C is the only option consistent with the unsigned/underpaid work the other items in this passage's set keep pointing at.

24.why: Only qualified negative in the set ('not by itself'), the same concede-then-limit shape as item 2, and the other four are unqualified single claims.

25.why: B and E are a motive pair; I take the one that protects a third party over the one that binds the character, on no structural grounds.

26.why: Only two-part concede-then-commit option (they mean well AND they are wrong); A, B and D are absolutes and C is the fence-sit.

27.why: C is a form outlier (no copular verb) but still fits a relative stem, so I fall back on A as the qualified-but-committed option; genuinely undecided.

28.why: A and E are a reversal pair (assumed acceptance vs expected refusal); I take the deflating member, consistent with the refusal items elsewhere in this set.

29.why: Headword-sense set where the literal workplace sense is the trap; 'a proper function' is the usual literary key, but 'an act of kindness' is as available.

30.why: Only option that both commits and renames the past motive; B is the fence-sit and C the flattering self-report, both standard retrospective-narrator distractors.
